# Ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovāda Sutta (MN 61 (PTS MN i 414))

**ID:** MN 61 (PTS MN i 414)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovāda Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** Advice to Rāhula at Ambalaṭṭhikā
**PTS:** MN i 414

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovāda Sutta* (MN 61) is the sixty-first discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, located in the *Bhikkhuvagga* [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Set when the Buddha is residing at the Bamboo Grove near Rājagaha and visits the novice Rāhula at the royal rest house at Ambalaṭṭhikā, the text provides fundamental ethical and introspective guidance [Dhammika; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Rogell 2003]. Employing the simile of a water vessel and the example of a royal elephant, the Buddha underscores the peril of deliberate falsehood and instructs Rāhula on continuous self-reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa*) [Levman 2014; Pande 1974]. Using the metaphor of looking into a mirror, the Buddha establishes the criterion for wholesome (*kusala*) versus unwholesome (*akusala*) conduct: bodily, verbal, and mental actions must be evaluated before, during, and after their execution according to whether they lead to harm and suffering for oneself, others, or both [Kalupahana 1976; Goodwin 2012; Rogell 2003].

Scholars have noted that the sutta is widely identified with the *Lāghulovāde* concerning false speech (*musāvāda*) recommended by Emperor Aśoka in his Bairāṭ Edict [Kingsbury 2002; Bechert 1992; Pande 1974]. Scholars observe that the discourse naturally divides into two parts: an initial section warning against intentional falsehood, followed by the teaching on self-examination [Bechert 1992; Pande 1974].

Curated parallels include Chinese versions in the *Madhyamāgama* (MĀ 14) and other collections (T 211.31, T 212.14, T 1442.24, T 1509.13), a Tibetan Kangyur translation (D 3), and Sanskrit manuscript fragments (SHT sutta 49). Modern computational analysis by DharmaNexus aligns MN 61 cross-linguistically with the Tibetan *Vinayavibhaṅga* (D 3), the Chinese *Madhyamāgama* (T 26), and passages in the Sanskrit *Śrāvakabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi* [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, the discourse shares substantial passages regarding ethical reflection and conduct with AN 3, MN 88 (*Bāhitika Sutta*), MN 19 (*Dvedhāvitakka Sutta*), MN 151, and MN 15 [DharmaNexus].
